en: §1 Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded and honored by a great saṅgha of monks, twelve hundred and fifty monks in all, as he taught the Dharma.

Now at that time, a lay follower named Nandika, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred lay followers, departed from the city of Rājagṛha and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and sat down to one side. Those five hundred lay followers also bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the lay follower Nandika addressed the Blessed One as follows:

Regarding those five precepts for a lay follower which have been prescribed by the Blessed One—the Tathāgata who knows and sees, the Perfectly Awakened One—what is the karmic result for one who transgresses them?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the lay follower Nandika: “Excellent, excellent, Nandika! Sublime is your intelligence; auspicious is your inquiry; beautiful is your inspired eloquence, you who consider it right to ask the Tathāgata about this matter. Therefore, Nandika, I shall teach you the Dharma discourse called ‘The Ten Disadvantages. Listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak to you. “Very well, Blessed One,” the lay follower Nandika replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this: "Ten disadvantages of taking life, beginning with Nandika, should be understood. What are the ten? They are as follows: enmity issues forth in this very life; there is a persistence of enmity in future births; one has unpleasant appearances; one sees evil dreams; one falls into terror oneself; one sleeps in suffering and wakes in suffering; one thinks evil thoughts; and one dies deluded."

He performs and accumulates karma that leads to a short lifespan; after the breakup of the body, following death, he is reborn in states of woe, in miserable destinies, in the hells. If, however, having passed away from there, he comes to this state of existence for the sake of the human condition, wherever he is reborn, there he will have a short life and much illness. Nandika, these ten disadvantages of taking life are to be understood.

§6 These ten, beginning with joy, are to be understood as the disadvantages of taking what is not given: one becomes an enemy of one's elders; one becomes suspicious of one's elders; one wanders at improper times; one is seized by evil friends; one is abandoned by virtuous friends; one becomes immoral; one is subject to calamities from kings, calamities from wicked beings, and calamities from punishment; and one performs and accumulates karma that leads to the ruin of wealth.

After the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in states of deprivation, in an evil destiny, in perdition, in the hells. If, however, having passed away from there, he comes to this state of existence for the sake of the common lot of human beings, wherever he is reborn, there he becomes poor and possesses few enjoyments. And whatever enjoyments he may have—devoid of enterprise and vigor, acquired through the strength of his legs and arms, and earned by sweat and toil—they become defiled by five secondary afflictions.

By which five? From the king, or from thieves, or from fire, or from water, or from unpleasant heirs; and his stored goods perish. These, Nandika, are to be known as the ten disadvantages in the taking of what is not given.

§7 These ten disadvantages of sexual misconduct should be understood. What are the ten? He incurs enmity with those whose wives he violates; he has disputes with his own wife; unwholesome qualities increase in him, and wholesome qualities decline; his person remains unprotected and unguarded, his life remains unprotected and unguarded, and his children and wife remain unprotected and unguarded.

His wealth remains unprotected and unguarded, and his home likewise remains unprotected and unguarded. His friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations do not place their trust in him. He performs and accumulates karma that leads to rivalry and enmity. Upon the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the states of deprivation, miserable destinies, and the abyss of hell.

If, moreover, having passed away from there, he comes to this state of existence for the sake of the common lot of human beings, if he becomes a woman, he obtains a husband who has co-wives; if he becomes a man, his wife and children remain unprotected. These, Nandika, are to be known as the ten disadvantages in sexual misconduct.

§8 These ten disadvantages of lying should be understood. What are the ten? His mouth becomes putrid; the deities depart from his body, and non-human beings find an opportunity to enter him; even when speaking the truth, his words become untrustworthy; when matters arise that require action, the wise do not consider him worthy of consultation; false disrepute spreads widely concerning him; and he becomes unworthy of being greeted by rising.

He experiences much suffering and mental distress. He performs and accumulates karma conducive to frequent false accusations. After the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in states of woe, in miserable destinies, in perdition, and in the hells. If, however, having passed away from there, he comes to this state of existence within the human community, wherever he is reborn, there he will be subject to frequent false accusations. Nandika, these ten disadvantages of lying should be understood.

§9 These thirty-five disadvantages of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants—the basis for negligence—should be understood. What are the thirty-five? 1. The immediate depletion of one’s treasury. 2. A source of diseases. 3. An increase in quarrels, disputes, and strife. 4. The exposure of one’s private parts. 5. The generation of ill repute. 6. The weakening of wisdom. 7. One does not acquire wealth not yet acquired, and wealth already acquired goes to ruin and exhaustion. 8. One reveals what should be kept secret.

His professional activities decline, and he becomes weak. He becomes disrespectful toward his mother; he becomes disrespectful toward his father; he becomes unfaithful to the ascetics; he becomes unfaithful to the brahmins; he does not honor the elders of the family. He lacks reverence for the Buddha; he lacks reverence for the Dharma; he lacks reverence for the Saṅgha; and he lacks reverence for the undertaking of the training. He fails to guard the doors of his sense faculties.

He falls into excessive negligence regarding women; he becomes untrustworthy to friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations; he becomes frequently unpleasant; he becomes disagreeable to many people; he practices unrighteousness; he fails to undertake his duties; he abandons the true Dharma; he abandons a sense of shame; and the wise do not consider him worthy of being consulted on matters requiring deliberation.

Having become negligent, he becomes indifferent; he does not abide in the words of the Tathāgata; he distances himself from nirvāṇa; and he performs and accumulates karma conducive to madness. Upon the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in states of woe, miserable destinies, perdition, and the hells. If, however, having passed away from there, he returns to this state of existence among the company of humans, wherever he is reborn, there he becomes insane and of confused memory.
Nandika, these thirty-five disadvantages are to be understood as residing in the state of negligence caused by *surā*, *maireya*, and *madya* liquors.
The Blessed One said this. Having spoken thus, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
One who is compassionate for the welfare of living beings should avoid taking life and the act of binding others;
just as you yourself protect your own dear life, so should you protect the lives of others.
Likewise, protect the life of others as well.
One should not even mentally covet the wealth of another, which has been accumulated with great hardship, nor touch it without it being given.
Even having seen the separation from loved ones in this world, one should likewise remain intent on the welfare of others;
and [one should avoid looking at] another's wife adorned with ornaments.
One should avoid her as if she were a blazing fire;
one should find contentment with one's own wife and not act like poison for the sake of desire. [3]
Neither for one's own sake nor for the sake of another,
one who possesses clear comprehension should not speak falsely;
he should not harm others and should not cause others distress.
Having reflected, one should utter sweet speech.
A person who delights in drinking intoxicants cannot achieve happiness for themselves or benefit for others.
One should not drink that *vāruṇī* liquor which causes delusion and discoloration, just as one would avoid the deadly poison of a young snake;
one should neither destroy life nor seize the property of others.
One should not speak falsehood, nor drink intoxicants;
one should not desire another's wife even in thought, if one wishes to enter heaven as if it were one's own home. [6]
O lady, these sinless ones dwell in houses where they have taken up residence, wearing only a single garment.
Furthermore, the Victor taught the instruction on the precepts and the teaching of the Dharma for one who has gone forth.

[7] Then the lay follower Nandika, having heard this Dharma-discourse from the presence of the Blessed One, was thrilled, satisfied, elated, and joyful; filled with gladness, joy, and mental well-being, he rose from his seat, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and, having rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had spoken, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, and with joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Noble Nandika-paripṛcchā-sūtra, the third, is completed.
